event: Aldous takes the questions straight, one at a time, as a man does who keeps a roll.
"Sulon. I told you that one. Osric is the king. Osric, second of the name, of House Sable."
"He's a name on the coin and on the tallies to me. Nobody here has seen his face."
"Lord Kell holds the vale. The king's steward for the north sits at Aldermere."
"I answer up through the lord and the steward. Never to the king himself. That's not my place."
Nala asks what's said of magic and monsters, out in the world at large.
He leans on the doorpost. It's an odd thing to be asked, and he weighs it before he answers.
"Every child here knows about mana. Cores. Skills. It's common talk, like the weather."
"You wake at fourteen and find out what you can do. Some heft a cart. Some heal a cut."
"I've little to speak of and I'm glad of it. Tobin the hunter's the only one here with more."
"Monsters are past the walls. The walls ring the plains, and nobody goes through them."
"Rifts open now and then. When one opens, soldiers come and the village empties out."
"I've never seen either one. Most of us die that way, and count it a good life."
He looks at her a while. "Being brought here by magic. That's no tale I've heard in Sulon."
"That's a thing for past the walls, or for a fever. I've no third answer for you."
Bess fills the doorway with a bowl in her hands. "Aldous Crane, she's barefoot in the cold."
She holds the bowl out to Nala. "Mutton. Eat it off my step if you won't come in the house."
Aldous says nothing either way about the bowl; he watches Nala's face over it.
"There's no bed for you here. I've a boy in this house and I don't know you."
"You'll sleep in the Sheaf's loft. Martha takes my word, and my word is you're here till morning."
He walks her across the green; the Sheaf's windows are yellow and the room inside is loud.
Inside is one long smoky room: trestles, a hearth at the far end, a dozen faces turning.
Martha Deane comes up from the stewpot with a ladle and looks Nala over, head to foot.
"Aldous Crane, what have you brought me?" "A stranger with no token. She answers for it tomorrow."
Martha sets a bowl of mutton and a hunk of dark bread on the nearest trestle in front of her.
The room goes quiet enough to hear the fire, and every face at the trestles turns.
"The fiddler's dead and the Sheaf's had nothing since. You say you can sing. Sing, then."
